title: Immune Responses in Endocrine Disease
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the immune system attacks endocrine glands and how hormones and immunity regulate each other. It covers Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes and its slow adult form, the autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes, the cytokine and cortisol feedback loop, and why conjugate vaccines protect infants against meningococcal disease and its adrenal complication. Board questions usually give a set of thyroid, glucose, or electrolyte findings and ask which effector (antibody or T cell), which antigen, or which tolerance mechanism explains them. If you can say whether an antibody causes the injury or only marks it, most questions in this unit become straightforward.
prerequisites: Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity types I to IV
Central and peripheral T cell tolerance, MHC class I and II presentation
Thyroid hormone synthesis and the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid feedback loop (EN-5, EN-8)
Insulin and glucagon secretion and C-peptide (EN-7, EN-8)
B cell activation, germinal centers, and class switching (IM-5, IM-13)

connections.how: Hashimoto thyroiditis is compared there with subacute and painless thyroiditis, using the uptake and antibody findings explained here.
The beta cell loss described here produces the absolute insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis of type 1 diabetes.
Neisseria meningitidis causes the adrenal hemorrhage of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome that conjugate vaccination prevents.
Graves disease is the model of a receptor-stimulating type II reaction and Hashimoto thyroiditis of a T cell mediated type IV pattern.
HLA-DR3 and DR4, CTLA4, PTPN22, AIRE, and FOXP3 explain why endocrine autoimmunity clusters in individuals and families.

sections.title: Graves disease: stimulating antibodies to the TSH receptor

blocks.text: Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. It is caused by IgG autoantibodies called thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) that bind the TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells and activate it. The TSH receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor that signals mainly through Gs, adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP, so the antibody reproduces the actions of TSH: iodide uptake through the sodium-iodide symporter, synthesis of thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase, hormone release, and follicular cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia. The gland becomes diffusely enlarged and highly vascular, and histology shows tall columnar follicular cells with pale, scalloped colloid.

In the Gell and Coombs scheme this is a type II hypersensitivity, because the disease is caused by antibody bound to an antigen fixed on the cell surface. Most type II reactions destroy the target, but in receptor-directed variants the antibody changes cell function instead: it stimulates the TSH receptor in Graves disease and blocks the acetylcholine receptor in myasthenia gravis. Susceptibility is linked to HLA-DR3 and to variants of CTLA4 and PTPN22, genes that set T cell activation thresholds, and women are affected several times more often than men.

blocks.title: Graves disease pathogenesis
steps: Loss of tolerance to the TSH receptor
IgG TSI bind and activate the TSH receptor
Gs and cAMP drive hormone synthesis and follicular growth
Free T4 and T3 rise; pituitary TSH is suppressed
Antibody stimulation ignores feedback, so thyrotoxicosis persists
blocks.caption: The stimulus comes from outside the feedback loop, which is why TSH is low while the gland keeps working.

blocks.text: Because the antibody is not regulated by feedback, hormone output stays high while pituitary TSH is suppressed. The typical pattern is low TSH, high free T4 and T3 (T3 is often disproportionately high because the stimulated gland converts more T4 to T3), and diffusely increased radioactive iodine uptake. Uptake separates Graves disease from thyroiditis, in which preformed hormone leaks from damaged follicles while new synthesis stops, so uptake is low.

Orbital fibroblasts and preadipocytes also express the TSH receptor. T cells infiltrating the orbit release cytokines that drive these fibroblasts to secrete hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans, mainly hyaluronan, and to differentiate into fat cells. The extraocular muscles and orbital fat swell and push the globe forward (exophthalmos). The same process in the dermis of the shin causes infiltrative dermopathy (pretibial myxedema). Because these lesions come from the autoimmune process, not from excess hormone, they are specific to Graves disease and need not track hormone levels.

TSI are IgG, the only immunoglobulin class transported across the placenta, carried by FcRn on the syncytiotrophoblast mainly in the third trimester. The fetal thyroid responds to TSH receptor stimulation from about 20 weeks of gestation, so high maternal TSI titers can cause fetal tachycardia and goiter and, after birth, neonatal thyrotoxicosis with irritability, tachycardia, poor weight gain, and goiter. The infant makes no TSI of its own, and maternal IgG has a half-life of about 3 weeks, so the disorder is transient and fades over about 1 to 3 months. Mothers with TSH receptor blocking antibodies can, by the same route, cause transient neonatal hypothyroidism.

blocks.title: Worked example: thyrotoxic newborn of a euthyroid mother
blocks.text: A woman had Graves disease treated by thyroidectomy 4 years ago and takes thyroid hormone replacement; her TSH is normal throughout pregnancy. Her son at 5 days is irritable and tachycardic with a small goiter, low TSH, and high free T4. Step 1: the infant's thyroid is being stimulated, because both free T4 and gland size are increased while TSH is suppressed. Step 2: thyroidectomy removed the mother's target organ but not her memory B cells and plasma cells, so she can still make TSI, and her normal thyroid tests cannot reveal them. Step 3: her IgG crossed by FcRn and now acts on the infant's TSH receptors. Prediction: the disorder resolves over weeks to a few months as maternal IgG is catabolized.

sections.title: Hashimoto thyroiditis: T cell destruction, antibody markers, and lymphoma risk

blocks.text: Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis) is the most common cause of hypothyroidism where dietary iodine is sufficient. It results from loss of tolerance to thyroid antigens, chiefly thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and thyroglobulin (Tg), the protein on which thyroid hormone is built. Susceptibility is linked to HLA-DR3 and DR5 and to CTLA4 and PTPN22 variants, and the disease is far more common in women, usually in middle age.

The injury is mainly cell mediated, a type IV hypersensitivity pattern. Three mechanisms combine. CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill follicular cells through perforin and granzymes and through Fas and Fas ligand. CD4 Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages that damage follicles. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies bound to follicular cells recruit NK cells for antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. The antibodies therefore add to the damage, but they are mainly a sign that the immune attack is under way.

The gland is diffusely enlarged, firm, and painless. Histology shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with well-formed germinal centers, small atrophic follicles, Hurthle cells, and variable fibrosis. As follicles are lost, T4 output falls and TSH rises, so the patient moves from subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal free T4) to overt hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4). Early rupture of follicles can release stored hormone and cause a brief thyrotoxic phase with low radioiodine uptake.

Anti-TPO antibodies are found in about 90% or more of patients and are the most sensitive marker; anti-Tg antibodies are found in fewer and are less specific. Neither proves the diagnosis alone, because anti-TPO is also present in about 10% of healthy adults (more in older women) and in most patients with Graves disease. In a patient with high TSH, anti-TPO identifies an autoimmune cause, and in subclinical hypothyroidism it predicts progression to overt disease.

blocks.title: Graves disease versus Hashimoto thyroiditis
rows: CD8 and Th1 T cells (type IV), with antibody-mediated cytotoxicity
Low TSH, high free T4 and T3
High TSH, normal then low free T4
Normal or low; low in the early thyrotoxic phase
Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, Hurthle cells, atrophy
Permanent hypothyroidism; primary thyroid B cell lymphoma
blocks.caption: Anti-TPO can be positive in both diseases; only Graves disease has stimulating TSH receptor antibodies.

blocks.text: Chronic antigen stimulation builds organized lymphoid follicles inside the gland. Continuous B cell proliferation in their germinal centers, where activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) drives somatic hypermutation and class switching, raises the chance of a mutation or translocation that gives one B cell clone a survival advantage. Primary thyroid lymphoma is rare, but nearly all cases arise in a gland with Hashimoto thyroiditis, at a risk many times that of the general population. Most are extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphomas or diffuse large B cell lymphomas, and the classic presentation is an older woman with known Hashimoto disease whose gland enlarges rapidly. The sequence parallels gastric MALT lymphoma arising in chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis.

blocks.predict: A woman has a high anti-TPO titer and a normal TSH. Is the antibody causing her disease, and what will happen to her TSH over time?
blocks.explain: The antibody mainly marks an ongoing T cell attack, although it contributes some antibody-dependent killing. A normal TSH means enough follicles remain to meet demand. As T cells destroy more follicles, T4 output falls and TSH rises, first with a normal free T4 and later with a low one.

sections.title: Type 1 diabetes: insulitis, islet autoantibodies, and LADA

blocks.text: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells that ends in absolute insulin deficiency. The strongest genetic risk lies in HLA class II: about 90% or more of patients carry the HLA-DR3-DQ2 or DR4-DQ8 haplotypes, whose molecules present beta cell peptides efficiently to CD4 T cells. Other loci include a repeat sequence upstream of the insulin gene that controls how much insulin is expressed in the thymus (and so how well insulin-reactive T cells are deleted), CTLA4, and PTPN22. Concordance in identical twins is only about 30 to 50%, so environmental factors, with viral infections the leading candidates, are thought to contribute.

The islet lesion is insulitis, an infiltrate made mostly of CD8 T cells with CD4 T cells, B cells, and macrophages. Autoreactive CD4 Th1 cells are activated by dendritic cells presenting beta cell peptides in the pancreatic lymph nodes and help activate CD8 T cells. In the islet, CD8 cells kill beta cells that display the same peptides on MHC class I, using perforin, granzymes, and Fas ligand, while interferon-gamma, TNF-alpha, and IL-1 add cytokine-induced beta cell apoptosis. The attack is antigen specific, so alpha, delta, and PP cells in the same islet survive. Glucagon secretion persists, and without local insulin to restrain it, glucagon excess adds to hyperglycemia and ketogenesis.

blocks.title: Progression of type 1 diabetes
steps: HLA-DR3 or DR4 risk plus loss of tolerance
Autoreactive T cells infiltrate islets (insulitis)
Islet autoantibodies appear; glucose still normal
CD8 T cells destroy beta cells, sparing alpha cells
Insulin and C-peptide fall as beta cell mass shrinks
Hyperglycemia when remaining insulin cannot meet demand
blocks.caption: Autoantibodies appear years before hyperglycemia, which appears only after most beta cell function is lost.

blocks.text: Autoantibodies arise as beta cell proteins are released and presented during the attack. They do not destroy beta cells: infants of mothers with type 1 diabetes receive these IgG antibodies across the placenta without developing diabetes, in contrast to the transplacental Graves disease of C01. They are, however, the best markers of the process. Risk rises with the number of antibodies, and children with two or more have a very high lifetime risk. This is the basis of current staging: stage 1 is two or more antibodies with normal glucose, stage 2 adds dysglycemia, and stage 3 is clinical diabetes meeting diagnostic glucose criteria. C-peptide, cleaved from proinsulin in equal amounts with insulin and absent from injected insulin, measures remaining endogenous secretion and is low.

blocks.title: Islet autoantibodies
rows: Glutamic acid decarboxylase, 65 kDa isoform (makes GABA in beta cells)
Most common in adults and in LADA; tends to persist
Often the first to appear in young children; interpretable only before insulin therapy, because injected insulin induces antibodies
Tyrosine phosphatase-like protein of insulin secretory granules
Zinc transporter 8, which loads zinc into insulin granules
Detects some patients negative for the other three
blocks.caption: All four are markers of autoimmunity, not effectors; the number of positive antibodies predicts risk better than any single one.

blocks.text: Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA, also called type 1.5 diabetes) is the same autoimmune process moving more slowly. Patients are adults, often over 30 and frequently not obese, positive for at least one islet antibody (most often GAD65), and do not need insulin at first, so they are easily mistaken for type 2 diabetes. C-peptide is preserved early and falls over months to years until insulin is required; a high GAD65 titer and multiple antibodies predict faster loss. Type 2 diabetes, by contrast, has no insulitis and no islet antibodies, and its insulin deficiency is relative, from beta cell dysfunction on a background of insulin resistance.

sections.title: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes type 1 and type 2

blocks.text: Central T cell tolerance depends on showing developing T cells the body's own proteins. In the thymic medulla, the transcriptional regulator AIRE (autoimmune regulator) makes medullary thymic epithelial cells express thousands of tissue-restricted proteins, such as insulin, thyroglobulin, and adrenal and parathyroid antigens. Thymocytes that bind these self peptides strongly are deleted. Without AIRE, T cells reactive to many organ-specific antigens leave the thymus, and several glands are attacked at once.

APS-1, also called APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy, candidiasis, ectodermal dystrophy), is caused by loss-of-function mutations in both copies of AIRE on chromosome 21, so it is autosomal recessive, begins in childhood, and is most frequent in genetically isolated populations such as Finns. The classic triad usually appears in this order: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis in early childhood, then hypoparathyroidism, then primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease). Two of the three establish the diagnosis. Ectodermal dystrophy (enamel hypoplasia, nail dystrophy), vitiligo, and ovarian failure are common additions.

The candidiasis is itself autoimmune. Patients make neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22, the Th17 cytokines that recruit neutrophils to mucosal surfaces and induce epithelial antimicrobial peptides. Mucosal defense against Candida depends heavily on this pathway, so infection affects skin, nails, and mucous membranes, while neutrophil killing in deeper tissue is intact and invasive candidiasis is not a feature. Neutralizing antibodies against type I interferons are present in nearly all patients and are a useful diagnostic marker.

APS-2 is far more common. It is defined by Addison disease together with autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, or both. There is no single-gene defect: it is polygenic, linked to HLA-DR3 and DR4 and to CTLA4, often affects several relatives across generations, begins in adulthood, and is about three times more common in women. Candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism are not features. A third disorder completes the comparison: IPEX, caused by FOXP3 mutation, is an X-linked failure of regulatory T cells (peripheral tolerance) with enteropathy, eczema, and diabetes in infancy.

blocks.title: APS-1, APS-2, and IPEX
rows: Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes
Enteropathy, eczematous dermatitis, early type 1 diabetes
Anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-22, anti-type I interferon, anti-21-hydroxylase
blocks.caption: Candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism point to APS-1; their absence with Addison disease and thyroid disease or diabetes points to APS-2.

blocks.text: Each gland's failure follows from the hormone lost. Without PTH, renal calcium reabsorption, renal phosphate excretion, bone resorption, and calcitriol synthesis fall, giving low calcium, high phosphate, and neuromuscular irritability. Adrenal destruction, usually with antibodies to 21-hydroxylase, removes cortisol and aldosterone. Low cortisol releases ACTH from feedback, and the POMC-derived melanocyte-stimulating hormone darkens skin and mucosa; aldosterone loss causes sodium wasting, hyperkalemia, and hypotension.

blocks.title: Worked example: a child with thrush, cramps, and darkening skin
blocks.text: A 9-year-old has had oral thrush and nail infections since age 3. She now has muscle cramps and carpopedal spasm: calcium 6.8 mg/dL (reference about 8.5 to 10.5), phosphate high, PTH low. Later she is tired and hyperpigmented, with sodium 128 mmol/L (about 135 to 145) and potassium 5.9 mmol/L (about 3.5 to 5.0). Step 1: low calcium with high phosphate and low PTH places the defect in the parathyroid gland, not in vitamin D or the kidney. Step 2: low sodium, high potassium, and pigmentation indicate loss of both cortisol and aldosterone with high ACTH, so the adrenal cortex itself has failed. Step 3: childhood candidiasis plus two endocrine failures is the APS-1 triad. Step 4: absent AIRE let self-reactive T cells escape thymic deletion.

sections.title: Cytokines, the HPA axis, and the anti-inflammatory actions of cortisol

blocks.text: Inflammation and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis form a negative feedback loop. IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha released by activated macrophages reach the brain by several routes: through circumventricular organs, where the blood-brain barrier is weak; by inducing cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) in brain endothelial cells to make prostaglandin E2; and through vagal afferents from inflamed tissue. Neurons of the paraventricular nucleus then release more corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and vasopressin, which raise pituitary ACTH, and IL-6 also acts directly on the pituitary and adrenal. ACTH increases cortisol synthesis in the zona fasciculata. The same cytokines and prostaglandin E2 raise the hypothalamic temperature set point, so fever and the cortisol rise start together.

blocks.title: Cytokine and cortisol feedback loop
steps: Infection or injury activates macrophages
IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha reach the hypothalamus
CRH and vasopressin raise pituitary ACTH
ACTH raises cortisol from the zona fasciculata
Cortisol blocks NF-kB and phospholipase A2
Cytokine and eicosanoid production falls
blocks.caption: Cortisol shuts down the same cytokines that called for it, limiting damage from the host's own inflammation.

blocks.text: Cortisol diffuses into cells and binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor, which sheds its heat shock proteins and moves to the nucleus. There it acts in two ways. In transactivation, receptor dimers bind glucocorticoid response elements and increase anti-inflammatory proteins, including annexin A1 and IkB-alpha, the inhibitor that holds NF-kB in the cytoplasm. In transrepression, the receptor binds the transcription factors NF-kB and AP-1 directly and blocks them, shutting off genes for IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-alpha, chemokines, endothelial adhesion molecules, inducible nitric oxide synthase, and COX-2.

Annexin A1 inhibits phospholipase A2, the enzyme that releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. Arachidonic acid is the common substrate of cyclooxygenase and 5-lipoxygenase, so cortisol lowers both prostaglandins and leukotrienes, and reduced COX-2 transcription lowers prostaglandin synthesis further. This is broader than the effect of NSAIDs, which block only cyclooxygenase and leave leukotriene synthesis intact.

blocks.title: Effects of cortisol on circulating leukocytes
rows: Demargination from reduced endothelial adhesion, release from marrow, slower exit into tissue, delayed apoptosis
Redistribution to marrow and lymphoid tissue, T cell apoptosis, less IL-2
Redistribution; reduced macrophage activation and cytokine output
blocks.caption: A high white count from cortisol is neutrophilic with low lymphocytes and eosinophils; cortisol deficiency shows the reverse.

blocks.text: These effects protect the host from its own response. In cortisol deficiency (Addison disease), cytokine production is unopposed, the blood often shows eosinophilia and relative lymphocytosis, and infection or surgery can precipitate shock. In cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome), the count shows neutrophilia with lymphopenia and eosinopenia, wound healing is slow, and bacterial, fungal, and opportunistic infections are more frequent because T cell function and tissue recruitment of leukocytes are reduced.

blocks.predict: A patient with Cushing syndrome and no fever has a white count of 14,000/microL (reference about 4,500 to 11,000) with 88% neutrophils, few lymphocytes, and no eosinophils. Does this prove infection?
blocks.explain: No. Cortisol demarginates neutrophils, releases them from marrow, and slows their exit into tissue, while it redistributes and kills lymphocytes and eosinophils. The pattern is expected from cortisol itself, so infection must be judged on other evidence; absent eosinophils actually fit cortisol excess.

sections.title: Conjugate meningococcal vaccines and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome

blocks.text: Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae type b resist phagocytosis because their polysaccharide capsules limit complement deposition and phagocyte recognition. Protection depends on IgG against the capsule, which activates complement on the bacterial surface. For N. meningitidis the main effector is lysis by the membrane attack complex (serum bactericidal activity), which is why people lacking C5 to C9 have recurrent neisserial infection; opsonization and splenic clearance also contribute.

Plain polysaccharides are T cell independent antigens. Their repeating epitopes crosslink many B cell receptors at once and activate B cells, mainly splenic marginal zone and B-1 cells, without T cell help. Polysaccharides cannot be processed and loaded onto MHC class II, so helper T cells never see them. Without CD40 ligand and T cell cytokines there is little germinal center reaction, and the response is mostly low-affinity IgM from short-lived plasma cells, with little class switching, no affinity maturation, weak memory, and no booster effect. Children under about 2 years respond poorly because their marginal zone B cells are immature and express little CD21 (complement receptor 2), which normally lowers the activation threshold when the complement fragment C3d coats the polysaccharide.

Conjugation applies the hapten-carrier principle. The capsular polysaccharide is covalently linked to a protein carrier such as tetanus toxoid, diphtheria toxoid, or CRM197 (a nontoxic mutant of diphtheria toxin). A B cell whose receptor binds the polysaccharide internalizes the whole conjugate, digests the protein, and presents carrier peptides on MHC class II. Carrier-specific helper T cells recognize these peptides and give help to that B cell (linked recognition), so the antibody it makes is still against the polysaccharide but now has the features of a T cell dependent response. The response works in infants, and the IgG also reduces nasopharyngeal carriage, which protects unvaccinated contacts (herd protection).

blocks.title: How a conjugate vaccine creates memory
steps: B cell receptor binds the capsular polysaccharide
B cell internalizes and processes the protein carrier
Carrier peptides presented on MHC class II
Helper T cell CD40 ligand and cytokines activate the B cell
Germinal center: class switching to IgG, affinity maturation
Long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells against the capsule
blocks.caption: The T cell recognizes the carrier, but the antibody targets the polysaccharide because the B cell chose the antigen.

blocks.title: Plain polysaccharide versus conjugate vaccine
blocks.caption: The antibody target is the same capsule in both; only the help the B cell receives differs.

blocks.text: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal hemorrhage during fulminant sepsis, classically meningococcemia. N. meningitidis sheds lipooligosaccharide (endotoxin) in outer membrane blebs, which drives massive TNF-alpha and IL-1 release, endothelial injury, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The richly vascular adrenals hemorrhage, adding acute adrenal insufficiency to septic shock and removing the cortisol brake described in C05 when it is most needed. Vaccination prevents the syndrome by preventing invasive meningococcal disease. Conjugate vaccines cover serogroups A, C, W, and Y; the serogroup B capsule resembles polysialic acid on human neural cell adhesion molecule, is tolerated as self, and is poorly immunogenic, so serogroup B vaccines use surface proteins instead.

blocks.predict: Why would a plain meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine given at 6 months fail to protect, while the same polysaccharide conjugated to tetanus toxoid succeeds?
blocks.explain: At 6 months, marginal zone B cells are immature, so a T cell independent antigen gives little antibody and no memory. The conjugate lets the polysaccharide-specific B cell present tetanus peptides to helper T cells, which drive germinal center class switching to IgG and memory against the capsule.

integration.text: The same tolerance machinery explains every disease in this chapter. HLA class II alleles decide which self peptides are shown to CD4 T cells, AIRE decides which tissue proteins are shown in the thymus, and FOXP3 regulatory T cells and CTLA4 restrain cells that escape, so defects at any level cluster autoimmune disease across the thyroid, islets, adrenal, and parathyroid. Pathology then depends on the effector. A stimulating IgG (Graves disease) causes hyperfunction and can cross the placenta, while T cell destruction (Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune Addison disease) causes hypofunction, with antibodies serving as markers. The anatomy of the hormone loss, from PTH to cortisol, predicts the laboratory findings.

Endocrine and immune systems also regulate each other in health. Cytokines activate the HPA axis and cortisol limits the cytokine response, so adrenal failure from autoimmunity or meningococcal hemorrhage leaves inflammation unchecked. Microbiology and immunology meet in vaccine design: the conjugate vaccine works because polysaccharides cannot enter the MHC class II pathway on their own. Limits apply: antibody prevalence figures vary between populations and assays, a positive marker shows autoimmunity but not necessarily disease, and some patients with clinical type 1 diabetes or Hashimoto disease are antibody negative.

summary: Graves disease is a receptor-stimulating type II hypersensitivity: IgG TSI activate the TSH receptor, giving low TSH, high free T4 and T3, and diffusely high radioiodine uptake.
TSI cross the placenta through FcRn and cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis that resolves over weeks to months as maternal IgG is cleared, even if the mother's thyroid was removed.
In Hashimoto thyroiditis the gland is destroyed mainly by CD8 and Th1 T cells; anti-TPO (most sensitive) and anti-Tg mark the attack and add antibody-dependent killing.
Chronic germinal center activity in Hashimoto thyroiditis underlies primary thyroid B cell lymphoma, usually MALT or diffuse large B cell type.
Type 1 diabetes is CD8 T cell insulitis that spares alpha cells; GAD65, insulin, IA-2, and ZnT8 antibodies are markers, and two or more predict disease.
LADA is antibody-positive (usually GAD65) adult diabetes that initially needs no insulin and progresses slowly as C-peptide falls.
APS-1 is autosomal recessive AIRE deficiency (failed thymic deletion): candidiasis from anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-22 antibodies, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease.
APS-2 is polygenic, adult-onset Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes, without candidiasis or hypoparathyroidism.
IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha raise CRH, ACTH, and cortisol; cortisol blocks NF-kB, induces annexin A1 to inhibit phospholipase A2, raises neutrophils, and lowers lymphocytes and eosinophils.

Conjugating capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier recruits T cell help, giving class-switched IgG and memory even in infants and preventing meningococcal sepsis and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

verify: Some sources classify receptor-stimulating antibodies (Graves disease) as a separate type V hypersensitivity; this chapter follows the competency wording and standard texts in calling it type II. Confirm the label NABNE expects.
The frequency of neonatal thyrotoxicosis in infants of mothers with Graves disease is quoted from about 1% to 5%; it is not stated here and should be confirmed if tested.
Anti-TPO prevalence in Hashimoto thyroiditis (about 90% or more) and anti-Tg prevalence vary with assay and population; anti-TPO in about 10% of healthy adults is an approximate consensus figure.
The magnitude of thyroid lymphoma risk in Hashimoto thyroiditis is reported anywhere from about 40-fold to over 60-fold; this chapter says only many times higher.
HLA associations for Hashimoto thyroiditis are given as DR3 and DR5 in Robbins; other sources list DR3 and DR4. Confirm the alleles NABNE expects.

The fraction of beta cell mass lost at diagnosis of type 1 diabetes was classically quoted as 80% to 90%; newer data suggest less at diagnosis, especially in adults, so the chapter avoids a single figure.
LADA criteria (age cutoff of 30 or 35 years, insulin independence for at least 6 months) differ between professional bodies; the term type 1.5 is informal.

The definition of APS-2 varies: some sources require Addison disease, while others include combinations without Addison disease under APS-3. Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Schmidt and Carpenter syndrome.
Twin concordance for type 1 diabetes is quoted from about 30% to 50% depending on follow-up length.

The role of CD21 deficiency in the poor infant response to polysaccharide antigens is the standard explanation in immunology texts but remains one of several proposed mechanisms (immature marginal zone overall).
